scenario: AITA for visiting my son unannounced. | My son’s(19) in an university. He’s in a different city and lives in an apartment with 2 of his friends. Ever since he left(2 months ago) he just started ignoring me. I didn’t call him excessively, maybe once in two days. He’d hang up or not answer and text me later that he’s busy. Few days ago I was in the city for unrelated reason. I called him because I wanted to visit him but he didn’t answer so I just went to the apartment. He said that he’s just busy with studying and all that stuff and I should give him space when he needs it. He also said that it was weird that I just showed up unannounced.

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

Ever since he left(2 months ago) he just started ignoring me. I didn’t call him excessively, maybe once in two days. He’d hang up or not answer and text me later that he’s busy. Few days ago I was in the city for unrelated reason. I called him because I wanted to visit him but he didn’t answer so I just went to the apartment. I joked about the place needing a good clean and he just rolled his eyes. I asked him why he was ignoring me. He said that he’s just busy with studying and all that stuff and I should give him space when he needs it. He also said that it was weird that I just showed up unannounced.

Instead of showing up, you could’ve **asked how he was doing** without demanding a response. - **Judgmental tone**: His eye-roll at the "filthy" apartment suggests he **doesn’t want your criticism**—this could’ve been handled with **concern, not judgment** (e.g., "Hey, I noticed things are hectic. His "busy" might mean he’s **not ready for deep talks**—don’t take it personally. 4. **Offer support without pressure**: - *"I’m here if you need me"* (low-pressure) vs. *"You’re ignoring me!"* (high-pressure). --- ### **Why His Reaction Matters:** His annoyance isn’t just about the visit—it’s about **feeling unsupported in his adulthood**. Many parents struggle with this shift from **"parent as protector"** to **"parent as ally."** - **If he’s struggling**, he might need **patience and space** to open up. - **If he’s just testing boundaries**, he’s learning to navigate relationships—**your reaction will shape his future interactions with you**. --- ### **Final Verdict: <0> (Not AITA, but the *how* matters)** - **You weren’t wrong for caring**, but **how you expressed it** (unannounced visit + judgment) likely **hurt more than helped**. - **The bigger issue**: His withdrawal and the apartment’s state suggest **underlying stress**. Instead of reacting emotionally, consider: - **Giving him space** but **reaching out differently** (e.g., a voice note: *"No pressure to reply, but I’m thinking of you"*). - **Checking in on his well-being** without demands (e.g., *"I heard [university] is tough—how’s it going?"*). - **Addressing the apartment indirectly**: *"I saw your place looked busy—want me to bring groceries or help clean?"* (This shows care without criticism.) --- ### **What to Do Now?** 1. **Apologize for the unannounced visit** (not for caring, but for the method): - *"I shouldn’t have just dropped by—I should’ve asked first. I just wanted to see you and didn’t want to bother you. Next time, I’ll call."* 2. **Ask how you can support him** (without fixing his life): - *"You seem stressed—what would help you most right now?"* (This puts the ball in his court.) 3. **Observe his response**: - If he’s **defensive**, he may need **more space**. - If he’s **relieved**, he may have been **lonely** and needed connection. --- ### **Key Takeaway:** Your intent was good, but **relationships thrive on mutual respect**. His reaction isn’t about you being "wrong"—it’s about **how young adults navigate independence**. The goal isn’t to "win" the interaction but to **rebuild trust** through **consistent, respectful communication**. Would you like help drafting a message to him? Or strategies for future check-ins?
